input: Representative sampling is an absolutely essential, yet frequently underestimated, aspect of effluent monitoring, because every downstream decision, from process control right through to regulatory compliance, ultimately rests on the quality of the sample that was actually taken. One of the most important considerations is where the sample is drawn from: ideally, the sampling point should be located at a position where the stream is thoroughly well mixed, for instance downstream of a turbulent section or a bend, and downstream of the last point at which anything is added to or removed from the stream, so that the liquid passing the probe is as homogeneous as possible. A probe thrust into a stagnant corner or a slowly moving layer near the wall will, by contrast, faithfully report the composition of that unrepresentative corner rather than the stream as a whole. Equally important is how the sample itself is built up: best practice is to collect a series of small increments at intervals spread across the period of interest and to combine them into a single composite sample, because the composition of an effluent stream is rarely constant over time. Perhaps the most pervasive pitfall of all is the single grab sample, which captures the stream at one arbitrary instant and can therefore be profoundly misleading: a grab taken during a washdown, a batch discharge or a production upset will dramatically overstate the average load, while one taken during a quiet period will understate it, and neither says anything reliable about the stream over the day as a whole. In short, the sampling point, the increment pattern and the compositing together determine whether the laboratory result describes the effluent itself or merely the moment and the corner at which someone happened to dip a bottle into it.
target: A sample result is used as the composition of the whole effluent stream, and the sampling procedure decides whether that substitution is justified. The sampling point stands where the stream is mixed: in a turbulent reach, downstream of the last addition or withdrawal, with the probe in the moving body of the liquid. A point in a stagnant corner or in a slow layer near the wall returns the composition of that corner, and a settled or stratified stream returns the composition of the layer the probe happens to reach. One sample is built from increments, small portions drawn at intervals across the period the sample is to represent and combined before analysis. Effluent composition varies with the production cycle, with washdowns, batch discharges and upsets passing as slugs, and the increments spread the sampling across that variation instead of concentrating it at one point in the cycle. A single grab sample takes the stream at one instant. Drawn during a discharge, the grab overstates the average load; drawn in a quiet interval, it understates the load; and in neither case does the result carry any information about the stream outside the moment of sampling. The defect is not in the analysis but in the sample: the laboratory measures the bottle it receives, accurately or not, and no accuracy in the measurement repairs a sample that never represented the stream. Where a permit limit applies, the limit is a property of the site permit; the sampling procedure is judged by whether the composite, as built, matches the stream over the period the permit examines. Increments, mixing at the point, and a probe in the moving liquid are the three elements that make it match. The increments are also preserved and handled as the analysis requires, since a composite that degrades or separates in the bottle between collection and analysis carries the same defect as a badly sited probe: the measured liquid is no longer the liquid that was sampled.
